newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.S., Britain criticize U.N. monitoring in Iraq.
newsitem.headline: U.S., Britain criticize U.N. monitoring in Iraq.

text.p: U.S. and British officials said on Wednesday the United Nations could improve monitoring of the Iraq oil-for-food plan, contending reports to the council were often vague and omitted conflicts with Baghdad authorities.

"One of the points to which we attach importance is that there should be proper monitoring in the way these humanitarian supplies are distributed," British Ambassador Sir John Weston told reporters as the Security Council prepared to renew the programme for another six months.
"We would like to see rather more regular and detailed reports provided for the Security Council," he said.

Under the plan, which went into force Dec. 10 and expires June 7, Iraq has been allowed to sell $2 billion worth of oil to buy food, medicine and other necessities to help alleviate the effects of sanctions in force since its August 1990 invasion of Kuwait.
The oil-for-food deal is an exception to the sanctions which will not be lifted any time in the near future. Both the United States and Britain are voting for the renewal.
A senior U.S. official told reporters: "We want to know from the (U.N.) secretariat what their teams are doing, how they are operating."
He said the United Nations was slow in releasing funds for relief agencies designated to work in the north and had allowed Iraq to assume parts of the distribution programme.

The plan requires the United Nations to be in charge of distribution in the semi-autonomous north whereas the Baghdad government was to be in charge of supplies in the rest of the country, subject to U.N. monitoring.
After the renewal which will expire in December, the official said, "we won't allow a continuation of this kind of a programme if they aren't doing that aspect of the programme well."

Another U.S. official said that in one case, an Iraqi minister summoned U.N. observers to his office and told them what they could and could not do, but the United Nations did not report this incident or similar ones.
The envoys believe the U.N. Department of Humanitarian Affairs, given the monitoring task by former Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali, was not the proper body to handle it.

The agency was geared to helping disaster victims or refugees and was used to cooperating with local authorities, officials said, whereas with the Iraq oil-for-food deal, the United Nations had negotiated special rights for monitors.
